studies.Population: men aged 45-64 years in the Shanghai Cohort Study
studies.Smoking Status: both smokers and non-smokers included; adjusted for cigarette smoking
studies.Reference: Dietary soy and increased risk of bladder cancer: a prospective cohort study of men in Shanghai, China.
studies.Authors: Sun CL, Yuan JM, Wang XL, Gao YT, Ross RK, Yu MC
studies.Timing: exposure assessed at baseline interview (1986-1989) before cancer diagnosis
studies.comparison_type: daily soy consumption versus less than once a week
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: obtained through in-person interviews at baseline using a food frequency questionnaire

sample_size.excerpt: Briefly, 18,244 men aged 45-64 years were recruited between January 1986 and September 1989. As of December 31, 2002, 61 incident bladder cancer cases were identified.

cases.excerpt: As of December 31, 2002, 61 incident bladder cancer cases were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: Compared to men consuming soy less than once a week, the RR (95% CI) for those who consumed soy 1-<3 times per week, 3-<7 times a week and daily were 2.05 (0.80-5.29), 2.45 (0.89-6.76) and 4.61 (1.57-13.51), respectively (p for trend = 0.004), after adjustment for age, cigarette smoking and level of education. The soy-bladder cancer risk associations in smokers and non-smokers were comparable.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Compared to men consuming soy less than once a week, the RR (95% CI) for those who consumed soy 1-<3 times per week, 3-<7 times a week and daily were 2.05 (0.80-5.29), 2.45 (0.89-6.76) and 4.61 (1.57-13.51), respectively (p for trend = 0.004), after adjustment for age, cigarette smoking and level of education.

comparison.excerpt: Compared to men consuming soy less than once a week

design.excerpt: we examined the association in a second, geographically distinct prospective cohort of Chinese subjects, the Shanghai Cohort Study

timing.excerpt: Information on soy consumption was obtained through in-person interviews at baseline

continent.excerpt: prospective cohort of Chinese subjects, the Shanghai Cohort Study
